entry.title: Box Office: ‘You Can See Everything’ Beats ‘Clayface’ to Capture First Place
entry.summary: 'You Can See Everything' takes first place at the box office, crosses $60 million domestically.
entry.content:
“You Can See Everything,” A24’s buzzy documentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes, has narrowly defeated Warner Bros. and DC Studios’ “Clayface” at the domestic box office. It added $10.6 million to bring its haul to $63.9 million. That was good enough for a first-place finish, something that “You Can See Everything” pulled off for the first time in its third weekend of release.

“Clayface,” a body horror “Batman” spinoff, earned $10.4 million, bringing its North American gross to $44.1 million. The superhero adventure has earned $83 million globally. It cost $44 million to produce, a relatively inexpensive figure for a comic book adventure. The film is part of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s efforts to revitalize DC and make it a true competitor to Marvel. The duo’s first film, “Superman,” was a hit when it debuted in 2025, but “Supergirl” lost tens of millions and was excoriated by critics last summer.

Related Stories
Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves
Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range

Laika’s stop-motion film “Wildwood” earned $7.5 million to push its domestic total to $25 million and its global gross to $35 million. The film is adored by critics but carries a $100 million price tag, which means it will struggle to climb into the black.

Black Bear’s erotic dramedy “Wicker” earned $4.1 million from 2,374 theaters in its second weekend to push its domestic tally to $13.2 million. The studio bought the film out of Sundance for $2.5 million, so it stands to be a modest hit for the company as it gets into distributing its own movies.

Elsewhere, “Everest: The Other Side,” the new documentary from the “Free Solo” team of Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin, debuted in limited release with $1 million from 515 locations. National Geographic Documentary Films backed the picture, which is expected to be an awards contender. Another Oscar hopeful, Sony Pictures Classics’ “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” expanded its footprint this weekend, earning just over $1.9 million from 1,112 screens. That brings its domestic haul to just over $2.1 million. The indie studio is pushing John Turturro for a long-overdue Academy Award nomination.

After this weekend, “You Can See Everything” has supplanted Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” to become the 18th highest-grossing documentary of all time. It cost a mere $7 million to produce.

entry.title: Producer Titles Can Be Bought, but Real Creative Producers Take Them for Themselves
entry.summary: Producers Alison Owen, Carla Hacken, and Lauren Miller Rogen tell IndieWire about the importance of persistence in bringing films and TV shows to life
entry.content:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the producers panel, “Tangles” producer Lauren Miller Rogen, “Ghosts” and “Harlots” producer Alison Owen, and “Devil Wears Prada” producer Carla Hacken spoke to students and guests about everything from how they approach giving good, productive notes on a story to how they’re looking at the current, rapidly consolidating media landscape for actually getting projects off the ground.

But the thing that unites all their work, across all phases of production, is a persistence to muscle it past whatever obstacles and challenges lie in its path. And that’s something that’s been true for them since they got into the actual work of the producing business. Owen spoke about how her “degree” in producing is something she earned with a bunch of university students, but not by actually attending university. It just started with a conversation with someone who was attending the UK’s National Film School at the time.

Related Stories
Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range
The Arcane Knowledge Directors Wish They Could Summon

“This was the early ‘80s, when things were a lot looser, but they said, ‘There are no producers there. But if you want to learn about producing, go to Notting Hill, where the bus stops outside the Coronet in the morning and just stand there and get on the bus,” Owen said. “You would get out to the film school, and the students who were making their graduation films would want someone to come out and produce for them. And they didn’t care that you hadn’t done anything. I didn’t know what a call sheet was or what PAs were or anything. But they were happy to have a pair of hands.”

Being a willing pair of hands led Owen to a small village in the middle of Wales, working on a senior graduation project, and that on-the-ground, very-on-location work has stood her in good stead since. “Not only are you learning stuff, but you’re meeting your peers. So they were all people who wound up directing major studio movies, editors, cinematographers, people that I work with now, like John Mathieson, who — you know, we all slept on a mattress above a pub, and he now lights for Joe Wright,” Owen said. I always say to students, ‘Network with your peers. They’re the people of the future that you’re going to want to get jobs from or hire.”

Being tuned into what your peers are up to can also show you what’s possible. Miller Rogen had written the script for her first feature, “For A Good Time, Call…” years before, but it was seeing Lena Dunham’s work in “Tiny Furniture” that made her realize it was something she could make happen herself.

“I saw ‘Tiny Furniture,’ and I thought, ‘Well, I could do that.’ And so I took the movie from the big producer, and I emailed my team and my writing partner, and I said, ‘We’re gonna make this on our own, and I’m gonna star in it.’ And they were like, ‘Whoa.’ And I was like, ‘No, that’s what we’re doing,’” Miller Rogen said.

That conviction — and the key connections to some independent backers care of Miller Rogen’s brother who worked in finance — led to a $750,000 raise for the film’s budget. “We shot in 16 days. And then we went to Sundance, which is, of course, lucky to get into. But we got into Sundance and Focus Features bought it and released it, and it was in movie theaters, which would never happen now. But it was extraordinary, and I felt shock and pride and fear because it was gonna be big and out there,” Rogen Miller said. “But it was incredible, and I think these days, there are so many ways to get your project seen.”

“ I think you just said the most important thing for all of them is there’s so many ways for you guys to get your work out there now,” Hacken added. “The success of ‘Backrooms’ and all these YouTube horror shows should give you hope that, you know, write something good, produce something good, find a great story, and there are other ways to get it made than the way it used to be.”

entry.title: Michael Mann Accidentally Shoots Himself in Leg at Los Angeles Gun Range
entry.summary: Michael Mann is in stable condition after accidentally shooting himself in the leg.
entry.content:
Michael Mann, the director of “Heat” and “The Insider,” shot himself in the leg at a Los Angeles gun range on Saturday.

A spokesperson for the filmmaker said that “a weapon accidentally discharged while holstered resulting in a superficial injury.” Mann was treated at a local hospital for a wound that was subcutaneous and minor. He is being released. The event took place during target practice. Mann is an experienced shooter who has been practicing on ranges for decades.

A spokesperson for the Los Angeles said that officers had responded to a “shots fired” incident at The Range LA at roughly 4 p.m. An investigation determined that the shooting was “accidental.” TMZ broke the news of the shooting.

The 83-year-old Mann is known for directing gritty crime stories, many of which look at cops and criminals and are set in urban landscapes. He was nominated for an Academy Award for Best Director for his work on the 1999 journalism thriller “The Insider” and the film was nominated for Best Picture. Mann’s other credits include “Thief “(1981), “Manhunter” (1986), “The Last of the Mohicans” (1992), “Ali” (2001), “Collateral” (2004), and “Public Enemies” (2009). As a producer, Mann received an Oscar nomination for Martin Scorsese’s 2004 drama “The Aviator.”

Mann’s most recent credit was 2023’s “Ferrari” and he is about to shoot a sequel to “Heat” that is based on a novel he co-wrote with Meg Gardiner. That film will star Christian Bale, Leonardo DiCaprio, and Stephen Graham. Mann also helped create the ’80s TV hit “Miami Vice” and later directed a film version of the show.

entry.title: The Arcane Knowledge Directors Wish They Could Summon
entry.summary: As part of SCAD Savannah Film Fest's Behind Their Lens panel, directors told IndieWire about the areas of filmmaking they'd love to explore more of.
entry.content:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026.

On the directors panel, “Blue Heron” writer/director Sophy Romvari, “Josephine” writer/director Beth de Araújo, “Custom of the Country” director Josie Rourke, “The Good Daughter” director Steph Green, and “Toy Story 5” co-director Kenna Harris spoke about their different paths into directing — a fair amount of team sports — and how they approach everything from thinking about locations to communicating their vision clearly with different members of their crews.

Related Stories
Artisans Break Down the Tricks and Treats of Designing a Trojan Horse at SCAD Savannah Film Festival
What Genre Will Be Hollywood’s Next Big Trend? Watch IndieWire’s ‘Pitch Me’ Panelists Weigh in

But the panel also spoke about the ways in which film as a medium is constantly changing and skills they would like to be able to bring to future projects, and that all directors might want to be aware of.

Rourke, whose first feature film had the challenge of creating a sweeping historical scope for “Mary Queen of Scots,” has been thinking about how directors and visual effects artists can work better together since she had to drop some (digital) castles into some Scottish hillsides.

“I just knew it wasn’t working, but I couldn’t figure it out. And in the end, I called a friend of mine who’s a really good architect and said, ‘Listen, just pop into the edit,’ [to look at the castle assets], and he looked and went, ‘Yeah, that wouldn’t stand up,’” Rourke said. “It was really interesting because my body had a visceral fear of wanting to use that structure. It’s just an imaginary castle but [I knew] it was dangerous.”

Rourke’s instinctive awareness is something she’s since worked on trying to better communicate with VFX teams, but there’s even more nuance to how those discussions are had. “Some of the smoke and mirrors about [VFX choices] is about cost. So I don’t even know how to look at this and go, ‘Here’s how I would achieve that more economically,’” Rourke said. “I know how to cut costume or cut set or cut script or cut the schedule, but I don’t know how to be in dialogue that is sensibly and creatively managing the budget for visual effects.”

Harris, who has been embedded in the world of digital animation for years as a story artist before fusing into a hivemind with their fellow co-director Andrew Stanton to tackle “Toy Story 5,” still has things about the process they want to learn, too.

“I wish I understood simulation a little bit better because I want to learn how to talk about in a way that feels more collaborative. And the reason I say that is because there are certain things that even today in a really fancy studio like Pixar that are still hard to crack, visually,” Harris said.

One of those things is folds in clothing — the ability to create the sense of clothing moving along a character’s body naturally or bunching up around the elbow in a believable way, the seemingly simple but actually quite complicated to craft illusion of a hood lying against someone’s shoulders.

“If I was gonna say, ‘Hey, I really care about sleeve folds,’ I’m sure my producer, Lindsey Collins, would be like, ‘What? Why? Why, why would you care about that?’” Harris joked. “But artistically, I’m fascinated by it. We’re still relying on these physics-based engines for things like that, and when I look at a lot of 2D art, there are people who can design the hell out of just making clothing [work], it’s beautiful the way that cloth works on our bodies, and it’s just so hard to do on a feature scale. And so, I think it would be awesome if I understood simulation more technically because then maybe I would get closer to having a conversation of finally getting to see the sexy clothes folds that I’ve wanted my whole life.”

Clothing is something that’s both important and underrated in live-action, too. For as much and as proudly as “Blue Heron” is an indie film, it was the first time that Romvari had worked with a costume designer and saw the power of what having a creative collaborator in that department could do.

“It’s often seen as this very frivolous and just clothing and, you know, often is treated as just like a woman’s department and who really, you know, just put something on them. But I’ve learned so, so much through working with my costume designer, Maria [Katarina], how integral it is for continuity, aesthetically, but also for actors’ safety and comfort,” Romvari said.

Costume does a lot of silent work in “Blue Heron” since it is a period piece set in the late ‘90s (horrid thought) with sections taking place in a more contemporary timeline as well. The shift in clothing, and how characters feel about themselves through how comfortable they are in their clothes, articulates things that they themselves can’t quite say.

“Just so often costume designers are asked, ‘Can you just throw something on them?’ And now I understand the inner turmoil that they go through when they’re like, ‘Do you know how much time I spent dying that shirt and then using this artificial scrub to make it look like it’s from this other period?’ Just so much work goes into it that’s just not respected, and it’s so integral to what you see on screen,” Romvari said. “ So I think I’m just speaking up for costume designers. It’s a really important element that I think is undersung for its value.”

entry.title: Artisans Break Down the Tricks and Treats of Designing a Trojan Horse at SCAD Savannah Film Festival
entry.summary: Production designer Ruth de Jong, editor Sarah Broshar, and costume designer Amy Roth talk about the hidden touches they put into their crafts.
entry.content:
As part of the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking team presents “Behind Their Lens,” a series of panel discussions with some of the most exciting artisans, directors, and producers of 2026. On the artisans panel, “The Odyssey” production designer Ruth de Jong, “Paper Tiger” and “I Play Rocky” costume designer Amy Roth, and “Disclosure Day” editor Sarah Broshar spoke to students and guests about their process and approaches towards each of their particular corners of the giant puzzle that is putting a film together.

But there was one thing that united all of them, across their different creative disciplines, and that was the importance of (sometimes quite literally) climbing hilltops to create a sense of authentic surprise.

Related Stories
What Genre Will Be Hollywood’s Next Big Trend? Watch IndieWire’s ‘Pitch Me’ Panelists Weigh in
Watch the ‘Rehearsals for a Revolution’ Director and Editor Explain How Memories Can Help Fight Authoritarianism

If a costume designer can delight a director without being asked for something specific, then the movie is alive. If the editor’s intuitive sense of rhythm is working in harmony with the footage that’s been shot, then in a lot of respects the film is showing the post team what it wants to be. And if a production designer can build a Trojan Horse to the right scale and it falls down? Well, don’t panic. It can look even more weathered and accurate to the initial plan when it’s picked back up again.

“Obviously the scale [of the horse] came from me needing to fill it physically with the actors and the IMAX camera and [cinematographer Hoyte van Hoytema] and Chris. So that’s how we proportionally worked out and built several of them, then built a separate body of the horse to physically shoot that scene, lowered it into a tank, and shot that on a set near our city of Troy,” De Jong said.

But in addition to needing to half-drown Odysseus (Matt Damon) and his companions, an IMAX camera, cinematographer, and acclaimed director, some of the aspects that make the Trojan Horse truly look like it’s been in the wars came about organically.

“[For the opening], we mounted the horse to a massive trench plate and got a dredger. We dredged up really deep into the sand. We did a few tests a couple of days before. We put the horse in the waves. It took a beating. It fell. We had to rebuild it overnight to then shoot the next day. So the horse you are seeing in the film went through a lot before it got shot. It was very physical,” De Jong said. “Water always wins.”

But according to De Jong, the work of production design, even on projects without the grand scope of “The Odyssey,” is always the same. “ I feel deeply that if my sets are too obvious, I’ve failed because they should fade to the back and the actors should just be immersed in their worlds, and the audience should be lost in that world,” De Jong said.

This is as much the case for good contemporary costume design, where the clothes should just help us make judgments about the characters and feel the shifts in the story, something Amy Roth talked about doing almost invisibly in both “I Play Rocky” and “Paper Tiger.” With the former, Roth took a lot of cues not just from the existing material around “Rocky” and Sylvester Stallone, but about how the character of ‘Mike’ would feel about his body as he worked himself up into becoming Sly.

“He really was like three people,” Roth said. “Dressing him early on was taking hints from a future Sly and putting them in the way he dresses so that we can see the impetus of how ‘Rocky’ came to be. He was big into working out and he was very body conscious. So that silhouette was important to me and I was literally, like, layering clothing onto Anthony so that he couldn’t bulk up,” Roth said.

Meanwhile on “Paper Tiger,” Roth worked in a silent partnership with the sets in order to give the characters caught up in a mob scheme more or less agency. “The house was very beige, so I put the actors just so that the mother was in focus. And then in the end she starts to fade. She starts sort of matching the walls; the mother and father sort of fade into the background.  And that’s just me doing my thing. I don’t think I even discussed that with James [Grey, the director], but he would’ve liked it.”

What the director likes and how the director is responding gets very important in the edit, which is where Broshar’s developed a great read on Steven Spielberg over the course of their many collaborations.

“When you’re spending hours and weeks and months and years sitting in a room with somebody, you get shorthands. You don’t have to say words as much. You can just kind of feel a twitch. If I make a little twitch, Steven will look at me, like, ‘What? What are you thinking?’ You can tell,” Broshar said. “I think you’re just always trying to sit down and watch the movie or watch the scene like you’ve never seen it before. I always watch myself watching something, and I try to see if I’m feeling tense or if I am getting distracted or thinking about what’s for lunch — and that is a real red flag.”

One of the ways in which Broshar can help surprise herself and the other folks watching a cut is with sound, especially on a delightfully bonkers action sequence like “Disclosure Day” has in its train chase. “Like anything, it just takes patience and imagination, and you keep an eye on the timing of things — where and how do you want to see the train, how far away is it, when do we hear the train, how loud is it?” Broshar said. “ I have great assistants who do really good sound work, and I just kept asking them for more. They’d say, ‘We spent three days on this.’ And I’m like, ‘Great. Now spend three more.’ And let’s just keep [going] more, more, more, more. And then, you know, it all gets polished out as soon as great Gary Rydstrom and Bryan Chomier and their team come in with sound.”

Whether it’s sound, color, or the elements of nature themselves, it’s the surprises and flourishes that artisans build into their work that help each filmmaking department feel alive.

entry.title: What Genre Will Be Hollywood’s Next Big Trend? Watch IndieWire’s ‘Pitch Me’ Panelists Weigh in
entry.summary: At IndieWire's Future of Filmmaking Summit, a panel of executives and representatives explain how they look for breakout hits.
entry.content:
Everyone in Hollywood is always looking for the next big hit, but the process of actually finding one is a unique combination of art, science, and luck. There’s no one way to learn how to look for hits (or sell them to those who are searching for them), but listening to opinions from smart people at every step of the process is a great place to start.

At our Future of Filmmaking Summit in Los Angeles, a panel that included Erica Lee (president of production and partner, Thunder Road), Julien Levesque (agent, Gersh) Ayo Kepher-Maat (VP of acquisitions and productions, Independent Film Company), and Rachel Shane (head of film and television, Madison Wells) sat down with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang for a wide-ranging conversation about what it takes to find a breakout hit in 2026.

The discussion covered the actual art of in-person pitching, working with producers, the value of writing on spec, and even the next genre that might be poised for a comeback (spoiler: more than one panelist thinks it might be erotic thrillers). If you’re looking to build a film career at any stage of the process, the Pitch Me panel is a must-watch.

Check out the complete conversation in the video above.

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen. For more information, visit here.

entry.title: Watch the ‘Rehearsals for a Revolution’ Director and Editor Explain How Memories Can Help Fight Authoritarianism
entry.summary: At our Art of the Doc event, director Pegah Ahangurani and editor Arash Ashtiani went deep on one of the year's most acclaimed films.
entry.content:
Pegah Ahangurani’s “Rehearsals for a Revolution” is one of the year’s most powerful films, combining half a century of Iranian history with the director’s own personal story of being exiled to London. It all forms one powerful tapestry that begins with a single word: “Yad.”

The Persian word for memory and remembrance ties the entire film together, allowing Ahangurani and editor Arash Ashtiani to weave timelines together under the idea that memory is its own form of revolution. At our Art of the Doc event in Los Angeles, the duo sat down with IndieWire editor-in-chief Brent Lang for a wide-ranging conversation that began with the film’s opening word.

Related Stories
‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination
Carrie Coon on ‘The Liberation,’ Life After ‘White Lotus,’ and Why Hollywood ‘Places Limitations’ on Actors — ‘Screen Talk’ Podcast Interview

“I wanted to emphasize the act of remembering, because the central idea of my film is about remembering,” Ahangurani said. “I grew up in Iran and I’ve lived there my whole life, and I know very well that the authoritarians, including the one in Iran, they don’t only censor people. They also try to erase our memories, erase our past, and replace it with their own version of history. They try to rewrite it, and we shouldn’t let them steal our memories. I think remembering is one of the few things we have. We should remember our past, we should remember our victims, we should mourn them. Only after that can we start to heal.”

Watch the complete conversation in the video above.

National Geographic Documentary Films, part of a joint venture between The Walt Disney Company and the National Geographic Society, is committed to bringing the world premium, feature documentaries that cover timely, provocative and globally relevant stories from the very best documentary filmmakers. Its award-winning and critically acclaimed films reach 300 million people worldwide in 180 countries and 33 languages across the global National Geographic channels and direct-to-consumer platforms Disney+ and Hulu.

Recent films include the Emmy-nominated winner of the IDA Award for Best Feature “The Tale of Silyan;” Oscar® and Peabody nominee “Sugarcane;” Oscar-nominated and Peabody Award winner “Bobi Wine: The People’s President;” Emmy Award winner “Lost In The Jungle;” Oscar- and BAFTA-nominated “Fire of Love;” Emmy and Peabody Award winner “The Territory;” BAFTA nominees “The Rescue” and “Becoming Cousteau;” and Oscar- and BAFTA winner “Free Solo.” For more information visit films.nationalgeographic.com, or find us onFacebook,Twitter,Instagram, and YouTube.

entry.title: ‘Who Killed Alex Odeh?’ Review: A Scattered but Searing Documentary Examines America’s Tacit Acceptance of Anti-Arab Discrimination
entry.summary: The "unsolved" murder of a Palestinian-American civil rights activist is used to explore how anti-Arab bigotry became so normalized in this country.
entry.content:
Times change, the arc of the moral universe bends towards justice, and yet one thing that has remained true for as long as I’ve been alive is that prejudice, bigotry, and explicit displays of racism have always been openly permissible in America — so long as they’ve been targeted at Arabs and/or Muslims. That sad and immutable fact was on full display throughout Zohran Mamdani’s mayoral campaign last year, and the say the quiet part out loud reaction to Abdul El-Sayed’s current senate race has somehow managed to be even worse on both sides of the aisle (Democrats lament that he “doesn’t share our values,” while Republicans straight up just call the guy a jihadist). But anyone old enough to remember 9/11 knows that it didn’t start with the likes of Vicky Paladino, just as I assume that anyone old enough to remember the assassination of Alex Odeh knows that it didn’t start with 9/11.

Related Stories
Carrie Coon on ‘The Liberation,’ Life After ‘White Lotus,’ and Why Hollywood ‘Places Limitations’ on Actors — ‘Screen Talk’ Podcast Interview
Netflix’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Won’t Play on Cinemark or Regal’s IMAX Screens

The sole fatality of a bomb that had been planted at the California office where he served as the West Coast Regional Director of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee (ADC), Alexander Michel Odeh was murdered on the morning of October 11, 1985, leaving behind his wife Norma and their three young daughters Helena, Samya, and Susan. To this day, his slaughter remains “unsolved.” And yet, as Jason Osder and William Youmans’ scattered but vital documentary “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” makes clear soon after it begins, there’s little doubt as to who was behind the killing.

Indeed, the film establishes that the case was effectively solved within days of the attack, and that all three of the primary suspects — all members of a right-wing terrorist group known as the Jewish Defense League — were only allowed to flee to Israel because powerful forces within the American political system preferred for them to get away with it. And to get away with it. And to get away with it. More than 40 years later, no efforts have been made to prosecute or extradite the presumptive murderers. One of them has even moved back to the United States.

And so, despite affecting the aesthetic and tropes of the true-crime format, “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” directly contradicts the expectations of its supposed genre. Instead of establishing a vast mystery for their movie to explore, Osder and Youmans — one of them Jewish, the other a Palestinian-American — give shape to the galling absence of one. Stunted and searching by design, their film unpacks the sociopolitical context of Odeh’s killing in order to illustrate how the easily Google-able question posed by its title could possibly remain “unanswered” for so long, and even partakes in some light subterfuge as part of an effort to pin down the culprits on camera.

What the documentary finds, or at least calls new attention towards, is alternately eye-opening, obvious, and eye-opening for its obviousness. First and foremost, Osder and Youmans use Odeh’s murder as a lens through which to examine the militarization of Jewish extremism at home and abroad (with an emphasis on the emergence of ultra-nationalist JDL founder Meir Kahane). Propelled by archival footage, the film has little room for personal reflection, but implicit in its focus is the willfully short-sighted extent to which “terrorism” has long been framed as an exclusively Muslim practice; Osder suggests in the press notes, but not the documentary itself, that American Jews are seldom taught about the more violent expressions of Zionism, an implication supported by my own memories of going to Hebrew School at a conservative New England synagogue.

“Who Killed Alex Odeh?” also examines how the tacit permission of such violence is what also allows it to ferment. That Israel welcomed Odeh’s alleged killers back to the holy land, and that President Reagan refused to recognize the severity of the hate crime they had committed against a fellow American on American soil (he never so much as sent a letter of condolence to Odeh’s widow), sent a clear and enduring message that the world’s most powerful governments were okay with the spilling of Palestinian blood. It’s since been alleged that Mossad and the U.S. State Department combined to shut down the murder investigation.

In the most harrowing sequence of a film that has little use for suspense, Israeli investigative journalist David Sheen disguises himself as an ultra-Orthodox Jew and meets one of the alleged killers while wearing a hidden camera — Baruch Ben-Yosef’s outspoken prejudices seem inextricable from his comfortable position as a pillar of his community. Later, when Osder lures him into a sit-down interview under false pretenses, Ben-Yosef excuses himself from the conversation when Odeh’s name is mentioned, his irritation softened (and made even more upsetting) by the “this again?” attitude of someone who seems to believe that no one could possibly still give a shit about the 1985 murder of a single Palestinian expat.

Somewhat diminished in the film’s erratic attempts to contextualize this ever-metastasizing sickness is Odeh himself. Born in Palestine but displaced to Egypt as a child because of the 1967 Arab-Israeli War, the righteous but mild-mannered Odeh dedicated his adult life to combating discrimination against his people in America. Home video footage and old clips from his television panel appearances paint Odeh as more of an egghead than a firebrand. He worked to make in-roads with the local Jewish community, and didn’t have much of a public profile aside from an occasional appearance on “Newsline.” During his final appearance on the show, he debated a member of the JDL.

Osder and Youmans also interview members of Odeh’s immediate family, whose “what is there to say besides the obvious?” has already been internalized by the rest of the documentary. A different and possibly more rewarding film might have done more to investigate the pain of living in a country that has all but signed off on the hate-based murder of your husband or father, but “Who Killed Alex Odeh?” has little patience for investigations. The only thing more obvious than the identity of Odeh’s murderers is the continued lack of political will to hold them accountable. And a country that lacks the political will to address the slaughter of one Palestinian is a country that lacks the political will to address the slaughter of Palestine itself.

Grade: B

“Who Killed Alex Odeh?” is now playing in theaters.

entry.title: Carrie Coon on ‘The Liberation,’ Life After ‘White Lotus,’ and Why Hollywood ‘Places Limitations’ on Actors — ‘Screen Talk’ Podcast Interview
entry.summary: Carrie Coon joins IndieWire's 'Screen Talk' podcast to talk her new film 'The Liberation,' life after 'The White Lotus,' and much more.
entry.content:
One thing I know is true: You want Carrie Coon on your podcast.

The Emmy-nominated “White Lotus,” “Gilded Age,” and “The Leftovers” star has made plenty of impact on TV playing strong-willed characters. But she’s also a magnetic presence on the big screen, from films like Sean Durkin’s sizzling ’80s marriage satire “The Nest” and Azazel Jacobs’ Bergmanesque sibling drama “His Three Daughters” to her latest film, Guy Nattiv’s “The Liberation.” In this film, she’s more vulnerable onscreen than ever.

But as dark as Coon can go — in the ’80s-set “The Liberation,” she plays a repressed, PTSD-addled Holocaust survivor brought under the sway of a hypnotic cult leader played by Lily James — she’s a delight to chat with. No topics are off limits. She joined this week’s episode of IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast to dive into “The Liberation,” but also to talk about life after “White Lotus” as an actor who is (her joke!) “top of the B list.”

Related Stories
Netflix’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Won’t Play on Cinemark or Regal’s IMAX Screens
‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Review: India’s National Epic Gets a Fittingly Massive Cinematic Treatment

“What I mean is if there are five films coming out in a year that have female leads, we know the five actresses who will be asked to play those parts,” Coon said. ‘And they’re warranted, they’re very talented, they deserve to be in that position. That just means, though, because there are so few, there aren’t very many left over for the rest of us to take a crack at. So it is unusual for me to get this opportunity. I had an opportunity to play the lead in a mainstream film, which was ‘The Nest’ … and it came out during COVID, and nobody saw it. And so it didn’t necessarily open the doors we hoped. Showing I could carry a film, that didn’t really happen for me with ‘The Nest.’ And so it was just very flattering to get a script [for ‘The Liberation’] like this come into my inbox.”

This time, though, Coon’s extraordinary performance in “The Liberation” could open the doors “The Nest” didn’t. (Distributor Bleecker Street is launching a qualifying run next week.)

Coon also talked about co-starring with her real-life husband Tracy Letts, who plays her “Liberation” character Rita’s husband in Nattiv’s film, and Letts’ infamously obsessive physical media collection — and how that’s trickling down to their two kids’ intrepid viewing habits.

Though first up, hear banter from me and my co-host Anne Thompson about our time at the Virginia Film Festival, awards season updates, and more.

Listen to the episode below or on your preferred podcast platform.

entry.title: Netflix’s ‘Cliff Booth’ Won’t Play on Cinemark or Regal’s IMAX Screens
entry.summary: Netflix's 'The Further Mis-adventures of Cliff Booth' won't play on Cinemark or Regal's IMAX screens when it opens this Thanksgiving.
entry.content:
Netflix‘s theatrical play was bound to have a few hiccups as it works through the kinks of putting movies in theaters for extended runs. One of its big upcoming releases, David Fincher’s “The Further Mis-adventures of Cliff Booth” starring Brad Pitt, won’t be playing at some major theater chains when it opens this Thanksgiving.

Regal and Cinemark have declined to play “Cliff Booth” on their IMAX screens as part of the film‘s IMAX-exclusive theatrical run beginning November 25, IndieWire has learned. For now, the film will play only on AMC’s IMAX screens worldwide, plus a few other smaller circuits with IMAX screens, bringing its worldwide screen total to about 550. AMC has about 200 IMAX screens in the U.S., which is the majority, while Regal has about 100 and Cinemark has closer to 20.

Related Stories
‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Review: India’s National Epic Gets a Fittingly Massive Cinematic Treatment
The 1973 ‘The Wicker Man’ Is a Classic, but Neil LaBute’s Loathed 2006 Remake Is Even Better

Those theaters will likely hold “Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” for a second weekend rather than play a Netflix movie that will be available to stream sooner (it drops on Netflix on December 23, in time for Christmas). Normally, IMAX dictates what titles will play on its screens, and theaters don’t have much of a choice, but in this case, because IMAX came aboard as a partner late in the game, IMAX allowed theater chains to opt out of “Cliff Booth” if they chose and would rather stick with “Hunger Games,” which it looks like they’ll do.

It’s a small letdown for Netflix, but there’s always a fight for premium IMAX screens, and moving “Cliff Booth” to Thanksgiving so it could have this IMAX-exclusive window was a big part of the thinking. Netflix had originally slated Greta Gerwig’s “Narnia” movie there, but it moved into February so that it could have a longer run in theaters and a clearer window at IMAX screens.

This isn’t even the only kerfuffle around screens and streamers that took place this week, as Puck, which originally reported the “Cliff Booth” news, added that Regal, Alamo Drafthouse, and also AMC are all among chains that are opting to not play Amazon’s “Ali G: Who Iz I?” as part of an “extended release” Amazon is planning for the film. That movie opened in just 150 select theaters last weekend as part of a brief theatrical stunt, and it’s dropping on streaming even sooner; though it never reported box office data for it, the Sacha Baron Cohen comedy is intending to continue its run, though the major chains are now opting not to hold it. Amazon did not respond to a request about how many screens the film will play on this weekend.

entry.title: ‘Ramayana: Rise of a Legend’ Review: India’s National Epic Gets a Fittingly Massive Cinematic Treatment
entry.summary: Read our review of the new Bollywood movie 'Ramayana: Rise of a Legend.'
entry.content:
In the hours before the review embargo for “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” lifts, Google should see a massive influx of searches for “synonyms for epic.” It’s a reductive label: if you’re even remotely interested in a three-hour movie that covers half of a 1,500 page book spanning decades of war, romance, revenge, and interactions with the gods themselves, you already know that it’s an epic. But it nevertheless bears repeating and underlining, or at least replacing with all the variations of “majestic” and “monumental” that a thesaurus can provide.

It’s hard to overstate just how big Nitesh Tiwari’s adaptation of India’s national epic really is. This is a film where Brahma himself, the Creator of the entire universe, makes an onscreen acting appearance before the 10-minute mark. Every facet of India’s topography, from lush grasslands filled with antelopes to gnarled forests with tigers and evil spirits lurking around every corner, is on full display. There are enough wars, musical numbers, “Gladiator”-style arena contests, talking eagles, lavish Indian weddings, Shakespearean feuds, da Vinci-esque flying machines, and shape-shifting to satisfy even the most attention span-challenged viewers. There are moments when Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey” looks like “My Dinner with Andre” by comparison.

Related Stories
The 1973 ‘The Wicker Man’ Is a Classic, but Neil LaBute’s Loathed 2006 Remake Is Even Better
‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: A Grieving Ski Mountaineer Scales the Face of Death in Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s Climbing Doc

In many ways, the bigness is the point. Along with the “Mahabharata,” the “Ramanyana” is one of two Sanskrit epics that all but define what it has traditionally meant to be Indian. The sprawling saga introduces many of the foundational tenets of Hindu spirituality and the storytelling principles that continue to inform all of Bollywood cinema. It might as well be Homer and the Bible all rolled into one, and Tiwari’s film adaptation takes that responsibility seriously.

When adapting an epic of this scale, a filmmaker can typically make one of two choices: there’s the route that Nolan took with “The Odyssey” of finding a specific angle within such a massive piece of material that allows you to put a personal spin on it. Or you can take a more generalist approach that aims to place the entire text on screen, even if it means sacrificing some specificity. This take on the “Ramayana” takes the latter approach, as Tiwari appears primarily focused on dramatizing the classic epic with the highest level of production value that’s currently available. He undeniably achieves that goal, even if it means that the final product lacks some voice that would have made it more memorable on its own terms.

The film opens with the world under siege by Ravana (played by Bollywood first-timer Yash), an evil king whose meditations were so intense that they threatened to destabilize the entire universe. To save everyone from imminent destruction, Brahma cuts a deal that grants Ravana immunity from any attack by humans, gods, or diseases. The caveat is that Ravana still isn’t guaranteed immortality, but it gives him a pretty big advantage over his enemies for the moment. He quickly takes over the world and introduces a dark age, prompting the god Vishnu to take on his seventh human incarnation as Rama (Ranbir Kapoor).

Rama is destined to become the legend who will right all of the world’s cosmic wrongs, but along the way he has to learn how to fulfill his worldly dharma by paying the price for his father’s sins. He ends up accepting a 14-year exile in the wilderness, where he is accompanied by his semi-divine wife Sita (Sal Pallavi) and his loyal (if occasionally insecure) brother Lakshmana (Ravi Dubey). They live a simple, dutiful life while preparing for a return to royal life — but the outside world does not stop plotting against them.

The intensity of those stakes, and what they mean to generations of Indians who grew up reading and hearing about Rama’s adventures, come through in every frame of the movie. “Ramayana” contains dozens of moments that would each be the climax of another film. It seems like every single scene features someone learning their destiny, meeting their true love, succumbing to their worst temptation, or winning their toughest battle. And each moment is scored with appropriate musical majesty by Hans Zimmer and A.R. Rahman, the former of which is lending his talents to an Indian film for the first time.

The only problem is that when every scene feels like a climax, you never get a chance to understand why each one matters. As silly as it sounds to call a three-hour movie (and a Part 1 at that!) too short, each of these turning points would matter a lot more if we spent more time with these characters in quieter moments. Truly great climaxes pay off endless amounts of waiting and yearning, but this take on the “Ramayana” is so jammed with excitement that we never have a chance to do either.

But perhaps that’s just a tradeoff that comes with being a legend. These characters have survived for centuries because they embody some of our greatest ideals and fears, and some of their immortality comes from our ability to see ourselves reflected back in two-dimensional characters. In moments when you struggle to invest in them, you can always sit back and enjoy the bright colors, swooping camera movements, and lavish orchestral score. Calling “Ramayana” epic may be a cliche, but there’s really no other word that would suffice.

Grade: B

Sony Pictures will release “Ramayana: Rise of a Legend” in U.S. theaters on Friday, November 5.

entry.title: The 1973 ‘The Wicker Man’ Is a Classic, but Neil LaBute’s Loathed 2006 Remake Is Even Better
entry.summary: In this Halloween edition of 'The Correct Opinion,' we argue that LaBute's Nicolas Cage vehicle is more complex and better made than the 1973 version.
entry.content:
Reader, you have been lied to! Film history is littered with unfairly maligned classics, whether critics were too eager to review the making of rather than the finished product, or they suffered from underwhelming ad campaigns or general disinterest. Let’s revise our takes on some of these films from wrongheaded to the correct opinion.

When filmmaker Neil LaBute signed on to write and direct a remake of the 1973 horror film “The Wicker Man” in 2006, both his fans and his detractors were surprised. Not that LaBute would be making a horror movie — after all, “In the Company of Men,” “Your Friends and Neighbors,” and “The Shape of Things” were all horror movies in a sense, disturbing pageants of trauma and sadism where the (human) monsters always won.

Related Stories
‘Everest: The Other Side’ Review: A Grieving Ski Mountaineer Scales the Face of Death in Chai Vasarhelyi and Jimmy Chin’s Climbing Doc
Bleecker Street CEO on Why the Social Media Suppression of ‘Musk’ Is About Much More Than Film

The surprise came in the type and scale of horror movie LaBute was making: a big-budget Hollywood movie with a big star (Nicolas Cage) derived from preexisting IP. Coming from a fiercely personal writer/director whose only previous studio assignment had been the handsomely mounted literary adaptation “Possession,” “The Wicker Man” seemed like an odd career choice.

Was LaBute just broke, or did he inject his own preoccupations into Anthony Shaffer’s tale of a policeman whose missing-person investigation on a remote island leads to his doom? I don’t know if he needed the payday, but I do know that the answer to the second half of the question was a resounding “yes.” Not only is “The Wicker Man” pure LaBute through and through, but it’s also, like Brian De Palma’s “Scarface,” John Carpenter’s “The Thing,” or David Cronenberg’s “The Fly,” a rare remake of a classic that’s actually superior to its source.

Not that people thought so at the time. LaBute’s movie failed to make its money back at the box office and drew almost universal scorn from critics, most of whom compared it unfavorably with the original (conveniently forgetting that the original itself met with mixed reviews upon release). LaBute was nominated for a Golden Raspberry Award for Worst Screenplay, which in and of itself should be a marker of the film’s quality given the Razzies’ consistent knack for being on the wrong side of history. (Other nominees in that category over the years have included Blake Edwards, Oliver Stone, Elaine May, Norman Mailer, and Lawrence Kasdan.)

As is so often the case, one of the very things that makes “The Wicker Man” great — its wild mix of tones — is also what made it misunderstood. The general consensus among those who didn’t get the movie was that it was silly and histrionic, that Nicolas Cage’s performance was over the top, and that scenes like the one where he infiltrates a cultish ceremony wearing a bear suit were ridiculous. Cage is over the top in the film, and the bear suit is funny. But why does this mean the movie is doing something wrong?

To the contrary, LaBute and Cage clearly know exactly what they’re doing, and the movie’s power comes from the collision between a sense of genuine horror and a layer of playful black comedy — the same combo that characterized LaBute’s acclaimed debut, “In the Company of Men.” That’s also a movie where laughs come in inappropriate places, but Labute got the benefit of the doubt as an unknown with no corporate support. For some reason, when he does the same thing in a major studio movie, people view the idiosyncrasies as “mistakes.”

The fact is that there’s as direct a line from a “pure” LaBute movie like “The Shape of Things” to “The Wicker Man” as there was from “In the Company of Men” to “Your Friends and Neighbors.” LaBute doesn’t just recreate the 1973 film; he reinvents it in ways that make it both more personal and more complex and resonant. The key alteration is that Cage’s cop character travels to an island dominated by a society of women. It’s a simple change, but it lets Labute extend and develop the inquiry into shifting power dynamics in heterosexual relationships that began with his first film and pervades nearly every film and play he ever wrote.

The persistent charges of misogyny that have followed LaBute since the beginning are so poorly argued they’re barely worth dignifying. They largely seem to stem from the idea that because men are mean to women in LaBute’s work, the work itself must be misogynistic. The quickest way to counter the argument is to simply watch “In the Company of Men” and “Your Friends and Neighbors” and ask one simple question: Who comes off most badly in these movies? Spoiler: It’s not the women.

While “The Shape of Things” does feature a woman who’s almost supernatural in her icy cruelty, taken in context alongside LaBute’s other work, I’d argue that if anything he’s a misanthrope and a cynic, not a misogynist. I’d also argue that given the Rachel Weisz character’s status as a kind of artist, “The Shape of Things” is as much a lacerating self-portrait as it is a statement about women — the movie is LaBute’s most potent examination of the ways in which artists justify the exploitation of their personal lives and their loved ones for the sake of their work.

“The Wicker Man” is admittedly the director’s most challenging film when it comes to defending him against the accusations of misogyny, but the view of women as manipulative and self-interested is counterbalanced by the movie’s often hilarious take on male superiority and anxiety. Like the detective in the original film, Cage arrives on the island puffed up with the authority his gender and position have given him, and LaBute takes undeniable pleasure in spending the rest of the movie stripping Cage of his power, security, and sanity.

This connects to another of LaBute’s big changes from the 1973 film: making Cage a troubled, compromised soul from the start. In the original movie, Edward Woodward plays the cop as a religious family man whose self-righteousness seems more or less justified. While this creates a starker contrast as the island residents taunt and torment him, it also makes for a less nuanced, interesting movie. Cage is already a mess when he gets to the island — the women just exploit what is already lying in wait beneath the phony masculine confidence on the surface.

LaBute’s shifts in emphasis make his “Wicker Man” more complex and rewarding than the 1973 film, effective as it is. Then there’s the question of filmmaking prowess. By virtually any standard, the 2006 “Wicker Man” is simply a far more aesthetically rich movie than director Robin Hardy’s unsettling but somewhat plain original, exquisitely lit and composed. (Among the movie’s few accolades was an award for DP Paul Sarossy from the Canadian Society of Cinematographers.)

LaBute has never really gotten his due as a stylist, possibly because his debut feature, “In the Company of Men,” had grain the size of basketballs and so little camera movement it made a routine episode of “Two and a Half Men” look like “Boogie Nights.” First impressions stick, and the impression “In the Company of Men” left behind was that of a great writer whose directorial style was basically just aiming the camera in the general direction of the actors to record them delivering his dialogue.

But LaBute was just getting warmed up. Shot on a production budget of $25,000, “In the Company of Men” was a film whose ambitions far outstripped its resources, and its director would never make a movie as technically ramshackle again. His follow-up, “Your Friends & Neighbors,” was modestly budgeted at $5 million but enabled LaBute to shoot in ‘scope and with precise care when it came to color, blocking, and rhythm. A professed admirer of Godard’s “Contempt,” LaBute would go on to rival that film’s formal elegance in virtually everything he made afterward.

That’s certainly true of “The Wicker Man,” a movie that fully utilizes its studio resources to create one expertly orchestrated frame after another. In the end, though, what gives the film its power is less its visual and aural flair than the deep sense of betrayal at its core. The cop’s ultimate fate in the original is motivated purely by economic necessity — he’s a human sacrifice the island needs for its crops to flourish.

This is true of the remake as well, but LaBute’s changes to Cage’s character, and his addition of a personal connection to the island, add a chilling dimension the original lacks. The movie’s final moments carry the same authentic sense of horror found in the betrayals that climax “In the Company of Men” and “The Shape of Things,” and the reversal is perhaps even more powerful coming in the form of an ostensibly commercial, mainstream movie.

Like Martin Scorsese’s “Cape Fear” or Spike Lee’s “Inside Man,” “The Wicker Man” is a genre movie given added potency by its filmmaker’s uncompromising sense of personal commitment. It also hints at what was to come in LaBute’s career, as he would ultimately lean into his knack for genre filmmaking — in recent years, all his movies have been thrillers or horror pictures, albeit with far fewer resources than “The Wicker Man.” “The Wicker Man” remains an artistic, if not commercial or critical, high point. Now that it just turned 20, maybe it’s time people finally acknowledged its virtues.
